questions.explanation:
Verbal Aptitude → Basic English Grammar

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Core Concept(s): Modal verbs expressing future possibility.
  • Given: A sentence with a blank: "I have not yet decided what I will do this evening; I ______ visit a friend."
  • Find: The correct missing word from the given options.

Solution

  • The first clause establishes that the speaker has "not yet decided", indicating uncertainty about their evening plans.
  • "might" is the standard modal auxiliary verb used to express a weak possibility or uncertain future action.
  • Analyzing the distractors:
    • would — implies a definite intention or hypothetical certainty.
    • didn't — is past tense (mismatched with "this evening").
    • mite — is a homophone meaning a tiny arachnid.

Final Answer

Answer: (C) might

questions.question: In the given figure, PQRSTV is a regular hexagon with each side of length 5 cm. A circle is drawn with its centre at V such that it passes through P. What is the area (in cm2) of the shaded region? (The diagram is representative)
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Mensuration and Geometry

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Area of a circular sector, internal angles of regular polygons.
  • Given: A regular hexagon PQRSTV with side length 5 cm, and a circle centered at V passing through P.
  • Find: The area of the shaded region in cm\(^2\).

Solution

  • A regular hexagon has internal angles measuring exactly \(120^\circ\) at every vertex.
  • Since V and P are adjacent vertices of the regular hexagon, the distance VP equals the side length, giving the circle a radius \(r = 5\) cm.
  • The shaded region inside the hexagon is a sector of this circle with central angle \(\theta = 120^\circ\).
  • The formula for the area of a circular sector: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times \pi r^2\]
  • Substituting the given values: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{120^\circ}{360^\circ} \times \pi (5)^2 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 25\pi = \dfrac{25\pi}{3}\]

Final Answer

Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{25\pi}{3}\)

questions.question:
A duck named Donald Duck says "All ducks always lie."
Based only on the information above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: Donald Duck always tells the truth.

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: Donald Duck always tells the truth.
structuredOptions.html: Donald Duck always tells the truth.

questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Logic

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): Self-referential statements and the Liar Paradox.
  • Given: The statement from a duck named Donald Duck: "All ducks always lie."
  • Find: The logically certain inference.

Solution

  • Assume Donald Duck is telling the truth. Then it is a universal fact that "All ducks always lie".
  • However, Donald Duck is himself a duck. If all ducks lie, then he must be lying right now — which contradicts the assumption that he is telling the truth.
  • Therefore, the statement cannot logically be true; it must be false.
  • The falsity of the statement means that not all ducks lie (some might tell the truth), but the only certainty is that Donald Duck's current statement is false.

Final Answer

Answer: (D) Donald Duck's statement is false.

  • Core Concept(s): Reflective symmetry across orthogonal axes.
  • Given: A figure of 20 unit squares with some black squares already present, and the requirement to add up to 5 more black squares.
  • Find: The minimum number of specific boxes to color black to achieve two lines of symmetry.

Solution

  • A line of symmetry divides a shape such that each part is a mirror image. Two lines of symmetry correspond to orthogonal vertical and horizontal axes dividing the grid into four symmetric quadrants.
  • For a grid to possess two lines of symmetry, any colored cell in one quadrant must be mirrored by colored cells in the corresponding positions of the other three quadrants.

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | GA Q6
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: Based only on the truth of the statement 'Some humans are intelligent', which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?
questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Logic

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Categorical syllogisms and logical conversion.
  • Given: The true premise "Some humans are intelligent".
  • Find: A logically certain inference.

Solution

  • In traditional logic, an I-type proposition (Particular Affirmative) takes the form "Some S are P".
  • A valid operation on an I-type proposition is simple conversion: "Some S are P" strictly implies "Some P are S".
  • Applying this rule: if the set of humans (S) intersects with the set of intelligent beings (P), then it is equally true that the set of intelligent beings intersects with the set of humans.
  • Therefore, "Some humans are intelligent" confidently infers "Some intelligent beings are humans".

Final Answer

Answer: (D) Some intelligent beings are humans.

Solution

  • In a negatively skewed (left-skewed) distribution, the tail is pulled towards extreme negative values.

  • Consequently, the relationship strictly follows the order: \[\text{mean} < \text{median} < \text{mode}\]

Final Answer

Answer: (A) mean \(< \) median \(<\) mode

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | GA Q9
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
Let \( a = 30! \), \( b = 50! \), and \( c = 100! \). Consider the following numbers:
\( \log_a c \),      \( \log_b a \),      \( \log_c a \),      \( \log_a b \)
Which one of the following inequalities is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): Properties of logarithms and inequalities.
  • Given: Values \(a = 30!\), \(b = 50!\), and \(c = 100!\).
  • Find: The correct ascending order of \(\log_c a\), \(\log_b a\), \(\log_a b\), and \(\log_a c\).

Solution

  • Since factorials grow rapidly: \(a < b < c\).
  • Terms where base is larger than the argument (\(\log_c a\) and \(\log_b a\)):
    Using the change of base formula: \(\log_c a = \dfrac{\ln a}{\ln c}\) and \(\log_b a = \dfrac{\ln a}{\ln b}\).
    Since \(c > b\), we have \(\ln c > \ln b\), so a larger denominator gives a smaller fraction: \(\log_c a < \log_b a\).
    Since \(a < b < c\), both values are less than 1.
  • Terms where base is smaller than the argument (\(\log_a b\) and \(\log_a c\)):
    \(\log_a b = \dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}\) and \(\log_a c = \dfrac{\ln c}{\ln a}\).
    Since \(c > b\), the numerator \(\ln c > \ln b\), so \(\log_a b < \log_a c\).
    Both values are greater than 1.
  • Stringing the inequalities together: \[\log_c a < \log_b a < \log_a b < \log_a c\]

Final Answer

Answer: (A) \(\log_c a < \log_b a < \log_a b < \log_a c\)

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
A square of side length 4 cm is given. The boundary of the shaded region is defined by one semi-circle on the top and two circular arcs at the bottom, each of radius 2 cm, as shown.

The area of the shaded region is _______ cm².
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Mensuration and Geometry

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Area equivalence and cut-and-paste geometry.
  • Given: A square of side length 4 cm. A shaded region bounded by a top semi-circle (radius 2 cm) and two bottom circular arcs (radius 2 cm).
  • Find: The area of the shaded region in cm\(^2\).

Solution

  • Total area of the square: \(4 \times 4 = 16\text{ cm}^2\).
  • The boundary features one protruding semi-circle on top and two inward-cutting quarter-circles at the bottom, all with identical radius \(r = 2\) cm.
  • By the principle of symmetry, the two bottom quarter-circle cutouts (unshaded) have a combined area exactly equal to the top semi-circular lobe (shaded).
  • Visually "cutting" the shaded semi-circle from the top and "pasting" it to fill the unshaded cutouts at the bottom, the shaded area forms a perfect rectangle covering exactly half the square.
  • Therefore: \[\text{Shaded Area} = \dfrac{16}{2} = 8\text{ cm}^2\]

Final Answer

Answer: (A) 8

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q11
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
For the integral
\[I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x^2} dx \]
which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Improper Integrals

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Integration limits from \(-1\) to \(1\), integrand \(= \dfrac{1}{x^2}\)
  • Aim: Determine convergence and value of the definite integral.

Core Concepts:

The integrand \(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\) is continuous on \((-1,0) \cup (0,1)\) but has a non-removable singularity at \(x = 0\) where it tends to \(+\infty\).

This is a Type-I Improper Integral. Convergence requires both one-sided limits to exist as finite numbers:\[ \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \left[\int_{-1}^{-\varepsilon} \dfrac{1}{x^2}\,dx + \int_{\varepsilon}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x^2}\,dx \right] < \infty \]Antiderivative: \(-\dfrac{1}{x}\).

Common pitfalls:

  • Incorrectly evaluating \(\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{1}\) directly (yielding 0) without handling the discontinuity.
  • Treating it as an even function and concluding a finite value — both approaches ignore the blow-up at \(x = 0\).

Solution Method:

Split the integral at the singularity, evaluate each piece using the antiderivative, then take the limit.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Write the improper integral as the sum of two proper integrals with a gap \(\varepsilon > 0\) at \(x = 0\).
  2. Antiderivative: \(F(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x}\)
  3. Left piece:\[F(-\varepsilon) - F(-1) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{-\varepsilon}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{-1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon} - 1 \]
  4. Right piece:\[F(1) - F(\varepsilon) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{1}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\right) = -1 + \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon} \]
  5. Sum:\[\left(\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon} - 1\right) + \left(-1 + \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\right) = \dfrac{2}{\varepsilon} - 2 \]
  6. Take the limit:\[\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \left(\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon} - 2\right) = +\infty \]The integral diverges to \(+\infty\).

Final Answer:

The integral does not converge | Correct Option: (D)

questions.explanation:
Concrete Technology | Creep of Concrete

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Behaviour of concrete under sustained compressive loading
  • Aim: Identify the correct definition of creep.

Core Concepts:

Creep is the time-dependent increase in strain under constant sustained stress (IS 456:2000, Clause 6.2.2).

The opposite phenomenon — decrease in stress under constant strain — is called relaxation.

Creep occurs at all stress levels; its magnitude depends on loading age, duration, humidity, etc.

Solution Method:

Common pitfall: Confusing creep with shrinkage or elastic strain.

  2. Options (B) and (D) describe relaxation (stress reduction at constant strain) — incorrect.
  3. Option (C) is physically incorrect (strain cannot decrease under constant compressive stress) — incorrect.
  4. Only option (A) correctly describes creep.

Final Answer:

Increase in the magnitude of strain under constant stress | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: A singly reinforced concrete beam of balanced section is made of M20 grade concrete and Fe415 grade steel bars. The magnitudes of the maximum compressive strain in concrete and the tensile strain in the bars at ultimate state under flexure, as per IS 456: 2000 are _________ , respectively. (round off to four decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Design | Limit State Flexure – Balanced Section (IS 456)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Concrete grade: M20
    • Steel grade: Fe415
    • Singly reinforced balanced section
  • Aim: Find the magnitudes of maximum compressive strain in concrete and tensile strain in bars at the ultimate limit state (IS 456:2000), rounded to four decimal places.

Core Concepts:

As per IS 456:2000, Clause 38.1 (assumptions for limit state of collapse – flexure):

  • Maximum compressive strain in concrete \(= 0.0035\) (constant for all grades)
  • Plane sections remain plane → linear strain diagram
  • For a balanced section, concrete reaches 0.0035 simultaneously with steel reaching design yield strain

Design yield strain in steel (for Fe415, cold-worked/HYSD bars):\[\varepsilon_{st} = 0.002 + \dfrac{0.87\, f_y}{E_s} \]where \(E_s = 2 \times 10^5\) MPa (IS 456:2000). Strains are dimensionless.

Solution Method:

Directly use the code-prescribed concrete strain and compute steel strain from the formula above.

Alternative verification: \(x_{u,\max}/d = 0.48\) (for Fe415) \(\Rightarrow \varepsilon_{st} = 0.0035 \times \dfrac{1 - 0.48}{0.48} \approx 0.0038\) (same result).

Common pitfall: Using working-stress strains (0.0020) or forgetting the 0.002 offset.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Maximum compressive strain in concrete (IS 456:2000):\[\varepsilon_{cu} = 0.0035 \]
  2. Compute \(0.87\,f_y\):\[0.87 \times 415 = 361.05 \text{ MPa} \]
  3. Compute \(\dfrac{0.87\,f_y}{E_s}\):\[\dfrac{361.05}{200{,}000} = 0.00180525 \]
  4. Tensile strain in steel at balanced failure:\[\varepsilon_{st} = 0.002 + 0.00180525 = 0.00380525 \]
  5. Round to four decimal places:\[\varepsilon_{st} \approx 0.0038 \]
  6. Verification:\[\dfrac{x_{u,\max}}{d} = \dfrac{0.0035}{0.0035 + 0.00380525} \approx 0.479 \approx 0.48 \text{ (as per IS 456 Table G-1.1)} \]

Final Answer:

0.0035 and 0.0038 | Correct Option: (A)

questions.explanation:
Concrete Technology | Mix Design

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application
  • Given Data: Variation in Water-Cement Ratio (W/C ratio) in cement concrete mix design.
  • Aim: Determine the relationship between W/C ratio, compressive strength, and workability.

Core Concepts:

  1. Abrams' Law (Water-Cement Ratio Law): The compressive strength of concrete is inversely proportional to the W/C ratio, provided the mix is of workable consistency.\[f_c = \dfrac{A}{B^{1.5(w/c)}} \]As W/C ratio \(\uparrow\), strength \(\downarrow\). Excess water creates capillary voids upon evaporation, weakening the concrete matrix.
  2. Workability: The ease with which concrete can be mixed, transported, placed, and compacted. Water acts as a lubricant between aggregate particles and fluidizes the cement paste.
    As W/C ratio \(\uparrow\), fluidity increases → workability (slump) increases.
  3. Reference: IS 456:2000, Clause 6.1.2 & IS 10262:2019.

Solution Method:

  • Analyze the impact of increasing water content on strength using Abrams' Law.
  • Analyze the impact on physical ease of movement (workability).
  • Correlate the two trends to select the correct statement.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Effect on Compressive Strength:
    By Abrams' Law, strength is inversely proportional to W/C ratio.
    Increasing W/C ratio → gel/space ratio decreases (more voids).
    Result: Compressive Strength Decreases.
  2. Effect on Workability:
    Increasing W/C ratio adds more lubricating water to the mix.
    Result: Workability Increases.
  3. Combined Finding:
    With an increase in W/C ratio: Strength decreases, Workability increases → matches option (A).

Final Answer:

Compressive strength decreases but workability increases | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: The specific gravity of a soil is 2.60. The soil is at 50% degree of saturation with a water content of 15%. The void ratio of the soil is ________ .
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Phase Diagram & Index Properties

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Specific Gravity: \(G = 2.60\)
    • Degree of Saturation: \(S = 50\% = 0.50\)
    • Water Content: \(w = 15\% = 0.15\)
  • Aim: Calculate the Void Ratio \((e)\).

Core Concepts:

Fundamental relationship between void ratio \((e)\), degree of saturation \((S)\), specific gravity \((G)\), and water content \((w)\):\[Se = wG \]

  • \(e = \dfrac{V_v}{V_s}\) (Void Ratio)
  • \(S = \dfrac{V_w}{V_v}\) (Degree of Saturation)
  • \(w = \dfrac{W_w}{W_s}\) (Water Content)
  • \(G = \dfrac{\gamma_s}{\gamma_w}\) (Specific Gravity)

Solution Method:

Rearrange the fundamental formula to solve for \(e\), then substitute given values.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. State the formula:\[Se = wG \]
  2. Rearrange for \(e\):\[e = \dfrac{wG}{S} \]
  3. Substitute values:\[e = \dfrac{0.15 \times 2.60}{0.50} \]
  4. Calculate:\[e = \dfrac{0.39}{0.50} = 0.78 \]

Sanity Check: For a medium-dense soil with 50% saturation and 15% water content, a void ratio of 0.78 is physically consistent.

Final Answer:

0.78 | Correct Option: (B)

questions.question:
A possible slope failure is shown in the figure. Three soil samples are taken from different locations (I, II and III) of the potential failure plane. Which is the most appropriate shear strength test for each of the sample to identify the failure mechanism? Identify the correct combination from the following options:
P: Triaxial compression test
Q: Triaxial extension test
R: Direct shear or shear box test
S: Vane shear test
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength & Slope Stability

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: A slope failure profile with three locations:
    • Location III: Top (Crest)
    • Location II: Mid-slope
    • Location I: Toe
  • Aim: Match each location to the appropriate shear strength test:
    • P: Triaxial Compression Test
    • Q: Triaxial Extension Test
    • R: Direct Shear (Shear Box) Test
    • S: Vane Shear Test

Core Concepts:

LocationPositionStress StateMajor Principal Stress \((\sigma_1)\)Appropriate Test
IIITop/CrestActive (Rankine)Vertical \((\sigma_v)\)Triaxial Compression (P)
IIMid-slopeShear along failure planeRotated (plane-specific)Direct Shear (R)
IToePassive (Rankine)Horizontal \((\sigma_h)\)Triaxial Extension (Q)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Location III (Top/Crest):
    The soil mass moves downward and away from the slope → Active State.
    Vertical stress is the major principal stress (\(\sigma_1 = \sigma_v\)); lateral stress is minor (\(\sigma_3 = \sigma_h\)).
    Best simulated by Triaxial Compression Test (P), where axial stress is the major principal stress.
    → III–P
  2. Location II (Mid-slope):
    The potential failure plane is parallel or sub-parallel to the slope face. Principal stresses rotate along this plane.
    Direct Shear Test (R) allows shearing on a specific pre-determined plane, which can be aligned with the slope failure surface.
    → II–R
  3. Location I (Toe):
    The sliding soil mass pushes against the toe → Passive State.
    Horizontal stress from the sliding wedge exceeds vertical stress (\(\sigma_1 = \sigma_h\), \(\sigma_3 = \sigma_v\)). Failure involves lateral compression pushing soil upward.
    Best simulated by Triaxial Extension Test (Q), where cell pressure (lateral) exceeds axial stress.
    → I–Q
  4. Match with options:
    Derived combination: I–Q, II–R, III–P → matches Option (A).

Final Answer:

I–Q, II–R, III–P | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q19

questions.question: When a supercritical stream enters a mild-sloped (M) channel section, the type of flow profile would become _______.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics & Hydraulics | Open Channel Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Incoming stream: Supercritical flow \((F_r > 1,\; y < y_c)\)
    • Channel slope: Mild (M)
    • Mild slope definition: Normal depth \(y_n\) is greater than critical depth \(y_c\) \((y_n > y_c)\)
  • Aim: Identify the water surface profile.

Core Concepts:

Classification of Surface Profiles on Mild Slope:

  • Zone 1 \((y > y_n)\): Backwater curve — M1 profile
  • Zone 2 \((y_n > y > y_c)\): Drawdown curve — M2 profile
  • Zone 3 \((y < y_c < y_n)\): Rising curve — M3 profile

Dynamic equation for surface profiles:\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{S_0 - S_f}{1 - F_r^2} \]

Solution Method:

  1. Determine the relative position of the incoming flow depth with respect to \(y_n\) and \(y_c\).
  2. Identify the zone.
  3. Determine profile behavior (increasing/decreasing depth).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Compare Depths:
    • Mild slope \(\Rightarrow y_n > y_c\)
    • Supercritical flow \(\Rightarrow y_{\text{incoming}} < y_c\)
    • Therefore: \(y < y_c < y_n\) → Zone 3
  2. Identify Profile Type:
    On a Mild slope in Zone 3, the profile is designated as M3.
  3. Verify Profile Behavior:
    • \(y < y_c \Rightarrow F_r > 1 \Rightarrow 1 - F_r^2 < 0\) (Denominator negative)
    • \(y < y_n \Rightarrow\) Velocity is high \(\Rightarrow S_f > S_0\) (Numerator negative)
    • \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(-)}{(-)} = +\) → Depth increases in the flow direction.
    The M3 profile is a rising curve (supercritical flow transitioning toward normal depth on a mild slope).

Final Answer:

M3 | Correct Option: (C)

questions.question: The direct and reversed zenith angles observed by a theodolite are \( 56^\circ 00' 00'' \) and \( 303^\circ 00' 00'' \), respectively. What is the vertical collimation correction?
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Theodolite – Vertical Collimation Correction

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Direct (Face Left) zenith angle: \(Z_1 = 56^\circ\,00'\,00''\)
    • Reversed (Face Right) zenith angle: \(Z_2 = 303^\circ\,00'\,00''\)
  • Aim: Calculate the vertical collimation correction.

Core Concepts:

For a perfect instrument, zenith angles from Face Left and Face Right satisfy:\[Z_1 + Z_2 = 360^\circ \]Any deviation indicates a collimation error. The true zenith angle is:\[Z_{\text{correct}} = \dfrac{Z_1 + (360^\circ - Z_2)}{2} \]The correction applied to the direct reading is half the total error.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Check expected sum:\[Z_1 + Z_2 = 56^\circ + 303^\circ = 359^\circ \neq 360^\circ \]
  2. Total error:\[\text{Error} = 360^\circ - 359^\circ = +1^\circ\,00'\,00'' \]
  3. True zenith angle:\[Z_{\text{correct}} = \dfrac{56^\circ + (360^\circ - 303^\circ)}{2} = \dfrac{56^\circ + 57^\circ}{2} = \dfrac{113^\circ}{2} = 56^\circ\,30' \]
  4. Vertical collimation correction:\[\text{Correction} = Z_{\text{correct}} - Z_1 = 56^\circ\,30' - 56^\circ\,00' = +0^\circ\,30'\,00'' \]

Final Answer:

Vertical collimation correction \(= +0^\circ\,30'\,00''\) | Correct Option: (D)

questions.question: A student is scanning his 10 inch × 10 inch certificate at 600 dots per inch (dpi) to convert it to raster. What is the percentage reduction in number of pixels if the same certificate is scanned at 300 dpi?

  • Aim: Calculate percentage reduction in number of pixels.

Core Concepts:

Total pixel count:\[N = (L \times R) \times (W \times R) = L \times W \times R^2 \]Since dimensions are fixed, \(N \propto R^2\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Pixels at 600 dpi:\[N_{600} = (10 \times 600) \times (10 \times 600) = 6000 \times 6000 = 36 \times 10^6\text{ pixels} \]

  3. Percentage reduction:\[\%\text{ Reduction} = \dfrac{N_{600} - N_{300}}{N_{600}} \times 100 = \dfrac{36 - 9}{36} \times 100 = \dfrac{27}{36} \times 100 = 75\% \]

Quick method: Since \(N \propto R^2\), halving the resolution reduces pixels to \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\) of original → reduction \(= 75\%\). ✓

Final Answer:

75% reduction | Correct Option: (C)

Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra – Non-negative Eigenvalues

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: \(M\) is an arbitrary real \(n \times n\) matrix.
  • Aim: Identify which matrix expressions always have non-negative eigenvalues.

Core Concepts:

Matrix TypeDefinitionEigenvalue Property
Symmetric\(A = A^T\)All eigenvalues real
Positive Semi-definite\(x^T A x \ge 0\; \forall x\)All \(\lambda \ge 0\)
\(M^TM\) or \(MM^T\)Always symmetric PSDAll \(\lambda \ge 0\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Option (A): \(M^2\)
    If \(\lambda\) is eigenvalue of \(M\), then \(\lambda^2\) is eigenvalue of \(M^2\). However, for complex eigenvalues (e.g., \(\lambda = i\)), \(\lambda^2 = -1 < 0\).
    Counter-example: \(M = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(\pm i\), so \(M^2\) has eigenvalue \(-1\). → NOT guaranteed non-negative.
  2. Option (B): \(MM^T\)
    \((MM^T)^T = MM^T\) → symmetric. For any vector \(x\):\[x^T(MM^T)x = \|M^Tx\|^2 \ge 0 \]→ Positive semi-definite → All eigenvalues \(\ge 0\) ✓ CORRECT
  3. Option (C): \(M^TM\)
    \((M^TM)^T = M^TM\) → symmetric. For any vector \(x\):\[x^T(M^TM)x = \|Mx\|^2 \ge 0 \]→ Positive semi-definite → All eigenvalues \(\ge 0\) ✓ CORRECT
  4. Option (D): \((M^T)^2\)
    \((M^T)^2 = (M^2)^T\), with eigenvalues equal to squares of eigenvalues of \(M^T\) (same as \(M\)). Same counter-example as (A) applies. → NOT guaranteed non-negative.

Final Answer:

\(MM^T\) and \(M^TM\) always have non-negative eigenvalues (both are symmetric positive semi-definite). | Correct Options: (B), (C)

Consider the following three structures:
Structure I: Beam with hinge support at A, roller at C, guided roller at E, and internal hinges at B and D
Structure II: Pin-jointed truss, with hinge support at A, and rollers at B and D
Structure III: Pin-jointed truss, with hinge support at A and roller at C

questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Stability of Structures

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Structure I: Beam with hinge at A, roller at C, guided roller at E, internal hinges at B and D
    • Structure II: Pin-jointed truss with hinge at A, rollers at B and D
    • Structure III: Pin-jointed truss with hinge at A and roller at C
  • Aim: Determine which structures are stable/unstable.

Core Concepts:

Structure TypeStability Condition
Rigid Body (Beam/Frame)\(D_s = 3m + r - 3j - C\)
Pin-jointed Truss (2D)\(D_s = m + r - 2j\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Structure I – Beam with Multiple Hinges:
    Total external reactions: \(r = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5\)
    Internal hinges at B and D: \(C = 2\) condition equations
    \(D_{se} = r - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2\); Net: \(D_s = 2 - 2 = 0\) (nominally determinate)
    Critical Check: Segments A–B–C–D–E with hinges at B and D create a mechanism with the given support arrangement. Insufficient lateral restraint between segments.

  2. Structure II – Truss with Hinge at A and Rollers at B and D:

    → Structure II is UNSTABLE
  3. Structure III – Truss with Hinge at A and Roller at C:
    Reactions: Hinge at A (2) + Roller at C (1) = \(r = 3\)
    Reactions are non-concurrent and non-parallel — satisfies necessary external stability condition. However, the member arrangement in this configuration leads to instability (deficient triangulation or improper geometry).
    → Structure III is UNSTABLE

IUnstableInternal hinges create mechanism with support arrangement
IIUnstableParallel roller reactions cause external instability
IIIUnstableDeficient member arrangement or reaction geometry

Final Answer:

All three structures are unstable | Correct Options: (A), (B), (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q29
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The probabilities of occurrences of two independent events A and B are 0.5 and 0.8, respectively. What is the probability of occurrence of at least A or B (rounded off to one decimal place)? _______________
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability and Statistics

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • \(P(A) = 0.5\), \(P(B) = 0.8\)
    • Events A and B are independent
  • Aim: Find \(P(A \cup B)\) — probability of at least A or B occurring.

Core Concepts:

FormulaExpression
Union of two events\(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\)
Intersection (independent events)\(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)\)
Complement / De Morgan's\(P(A \cup B) = 1 - P(\bar{A})P(\bar{B})\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Method 1 – Direct:\[P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.8 = 0.40 \]\[P(A \cup B) = 0.5 + 0.8 - 0.40 = 0.90 \]
  2. Method 2 – Complement (Verification):\[P(\bar{A}) = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, \quad P(\bar{B}) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 \]\[P(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B}) = 0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.10 \]\[P(A \cup B) = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90 \checkmark \]
Sanity CheckResultValid?
Probability range\(0 \le 0.9 \le 1\)✓
Greater than individual probabilities\(0.9 > 0.8 > 0.5\)✓
Less than arithmetic sum\(0.9 < 0.5 + 0.8 = 1.3\)✓
Independence consistency\(P(A \cap B) = 0.4 = 0.5 \times 0.8\)✓

Final Answer:

\[P(A \cup B) = \boxed{0.9} \]Accepted range: 0.9 to 0.9

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q30
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: In the differential equation \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} + \alpha x y = 0 \), \( \alpha \) is a positive constant. If \( y = 1.0 \) at \( x = 0.0 \), and \( y = 0.8 \) at \( x = 1.0 \), the value of \( \alpha \) is _____________ (rounded off to three decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | First Order Ordinary Differential Equations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Differential Equation: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \alpha x y = 0\), \(\alpha > 0\)
    • Boundary Conditions: \(y(0.0) = 1.0\) and \(y(1.0) = 0.8\)
  • Aim: Calculate the value of constant \(\alpha\).

Core Concepts:

Variable Separable Method: Rearrange to separate \(y\) and \(x\), integrate, then apply boundary conditions to find \(\alpha\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Separate variables:\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\alpha x y \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{y} = -\alpha x\,dx \]
  2. Integrate both sides:\[\int \dfrac{dy}{y} = \int -\alpha x\,dx \Rightarrow \ln(y) = -\dfrac{\alpha x^2}{2} + C_1 \]
  3. Apply first boundary condition \((x=0, y=1)\):\[\ln(1) = 0 + C_1 \Rightarrow C_1 = 0 \]\[\therefore y = e^{-\alpha x^2/2} \]
  4. Apply second boundary condition \((x=1, y=0.8)\):\[0.8 = e^{-\alpha/2} \Rightarrow \ln(0.8) = -\dfrac{\alpha}{2} \]
  5. Solve for \(\alpha\):\[\alpha = -2\ln(0.8) = 2\ln\!\left(\dfrac{1}{0.8}\right) = 2\ln(1.25) \]\[\ln(1.25) \approx 0.22314 \Rightarrow \alpha = 2 \times 0.22314 \approx 0.446 \]

Final Answer:

\(\alpha \approx 0.446\) | Accepted range: 0.445 to 0.447

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q32

questions.question: A drained direct shear test was carried out on a sandy soil. Under a normal stress of 50 kPa, the test specimen failed at a shear stress of 35 kPa. The angle of internal friction of the sample is ______________ degree (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength – Drained Direct Shear Test

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Test: Drained Direct Shear on sandy soil (\(c' = 0\))
    • Normal stress: \(\sigma_n = 50\text{ kPa}\)
    • Shear stress at failure: \(\tau_f = 35\text{ kPa}\)
  • Aim: Determine the angle of internal friction \((\phi')\).

Core Concepts:

Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion for cohesionless soil (\(c' = 0\)):\[\tau_f = \sigma_n \tan(\phi') \]In a drained test on sand, total stresses equal effective stresses (no excess pore pressure).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Apply failure criterion:\[35 = 50 \times \tan(\phi') \]
  2. Solve for \(\tan(\phi')\):\[\tan(\phi') = \dfrac{35}{50} = 0.7 \]
  3. Calculate angle:\[\phi' = \arctan(0.7) \approx 34.99^\circ \approx 35^\circ \]

Final Answer:

\(\phi' = 35^\circ\) | Accepted range: 35 to 35

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q33

questions.question: A canal supplies water to an area growing wheat over 100 hectares. The duration between the first and last watering is 120 days, and the total depth of water required by the crop is 35 cm. The most intense watering is required over a period of 30 days and requires a total depth of water equal to 12 cm. Assuming precipitation to be negligible and neglecting all losses, the minimum discharge (in m³/s, rounded off to three decimal places) in the canal to satisfy the crop requirement is ________________.
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Water Requirements of Crops

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Crop: Wheat; Area: \(A = 100\text{ ha}\)
    • Base period: \(B = 120\text{ days}\); Total depth: \(\Delta = 35\text{ cm}\)
    • Kor period: \(T_{kor} = 30\text{ days}\); Kor depth: \(\Delta_{kor} = 12\text{ cm}\)
    • Neglect precipitation and losses.
  • Aim: Minimum discharge \((Q)\) in the canal (m³/s).

Core Concepts:

The canal must supply the Kor depth during the Kor period — this peak demand governs the design discharge:

Average demand rate: \(\dfrac{0.35}{120} \approx 0.00292\text{ m/day}\)
Kor demand rate: \(\dfrac{0.12}{30} = 0.004\text{ m/day}\)
Since Kor demand \(>\) average demand, Kor governs.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Volume to be supplied during Kor period:\[\text{Volume} = 100\text{ ha} \times 0.12\text{ m} = 100 \times 10^4 \times 0.12 = 120{,}000\text{ m}^3 \]
  2. Convert Kor period to seconds:\[T = 30 \times 24 \times 3600 = 2{,}592{,}000\text{ s} \]
  3. Calculate discharge:\[Q = \dfrac{120{,}000}{2{,}592{,}000} \approx 0.046296\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \approx 0.046\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]

Final Answer:

\(Q \approx 0.046\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) | Accepted range: 0.045 to 0.047

questions.question:
The ordinates of a one-hour unit hydrograph for a catchment are given below:

t (hour)01234567
Q (m³/s)09211812520


Using the principle of superposition, a D-hour unit hydrograph for the catchment was derived from this one-hour unit hydrograph. The ordinates of the D-hour unit hydrograph were obtained as 3 m³/s at t = 1 hour and 10 m³/s at t = 2 hour. The value of D (in integer) is ___________.
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Unit Hydrograph – Duration Derivation

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • 1-hour Unit Hydrograph (1-h UH) ordinates given
    • Derived D-hour UH ordinates: \(3\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) at \(t=1\text{ hr}\), \(10\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) at \(t=2\text{ hr}\)
  • Aim: Find the integer duration \(D\).

Core Concepts:

Superposition Principle:\[UH_D(t) = \dfrac{1}{D}\sum_{i=0}^{D-1} UH_1(t-i) \]A D-hour UH is the average of \(D\) lagged 1-hour UHs.

1-hour UH Ordinates:

Time (hr)01234567
\(UH_1\) (m³/s)09211812520

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Test \(D = 3\):\[UH_3(t) = \dfrac{UH_1(t) + UH_1(t-1) + UH_1(t-2)}{3} \]
  2. At \(t = 1\text{ hr}\):\[UH_3(1) = \dfrac{UH_1(1) + UH_1(0) + UH_1(-1)}{3} = \dfrac{9 + 0 + 0}{3} = 3\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \checkmark \]
  3. At \(t = 2\text{ hr}\):\[UH_3(2) = \dfrac{UH_1(2) + UH_1(1) + UH_1(0)}{3} = \dfrac{21 + 9 + 0}{3} = \dfrac{30}{3} = 10\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \checkmark \]
  4. Both values match perfectly for \(D = 3\).

Final Answer:

\(D = 3\text{ hours}\) | Accepted range: 3 to 3

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: For a horizontal curve, the radius of a circular curve is obtained as 300 m with the design speed as 15 m/s. If the allowable jerk is 0.75 m/s³, what is the minimum length (in m, in integer) of the transition curve?________________
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Geometric Design of Highways – Transition Curve Length

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Radius of circular curve: \(R = 300\text{ m}\)
    • Design speed: \(V = 15\text{ m/s}\)
    • Allowable rate of change of centrifugal acceleration (jerk): \(C = 0.75\text{ m/s}^3\)
  • Aim: Minimum length of transition curve \((L_s)\).

Core Concepts:

Jerk Criterion:\[L_s = \dfrac{v^3}{C \cdot R} \]

Empirical Formula (IRC):\[L_s = \dfrac{2.7V^2}{R} \quad (V\text{ in kmph}) \]In practice, the larger of the two values is adopted.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Method 1 – Jerk criterion:\[L_s = \dfrac{15^3}{0.75 \times 300} = \dfrac{3375}{225} = 15\text{ m} \]
  2. Method 2 – Empirical formula (IRC):\[V_{\text{kmph}} = 15 \times 3.6 = 54\text{ kmph} \]\[L_s = \dfrac{2.7 \times 54^2}{300} = \dfrac{2.7 \times 2916}{300} = \dfrac{7873.2}{300} \approx 26.24\text{ m} \approx 26\text{ m} \]
  3. Selection: The jerk criterion gives 15 m; the empirical formula gives ≈26 m. In standard IRC practice, the minimum of the specified criteria is used, but the larger empirical value may govern as minimum. GATE accepted both values.

Final Answer:

\(L_s = 15\text{ m}\) (from jerk criterion) or \(\approx 26\text{ m}\) (from empirical formula)
Accepted range: 15 to 15 OR 26 to 27

questions.explanation:
Numerical Methods | Numerical Integration

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application (Visual interpretation and property of numerical methods)
  • Given Data: A function \(f(x)\) is shown in a figure. The curve is "convex-shaped" (bulging outward/upward), which is mathematically known as Concave Down \((f''(x) < 0)\). Method used: Trapezoidal Rule.
  • Aim: Determine if the numerically computed area is less than, greater than, or equal to the actual area.

Core Concepts:

  1. Trapezoidal Rule: This method approximates the area under a curve by connecting discrete data points with straight line segments (chords), forming trapezoids.
  2. Geometric Interpretation:
    • If a curve is Concave Up \((f''(x) > 0)\), the chord lies above the curve. \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{Area}_{\text{trap}} > \text{Area}_{\text{actual}}\)
    • If a curve is Concave Down \((f''(x) < 0)\), the chord lies below the curve. \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{Area}_{\text{trap}} < \text{Area}_{\text{actual}}\)
  3. Visual "Convexity": While the problem uses the term "convex-shaped", the diagram shows a curve where the slope is decreasing (inverted parabola shape), corresponding to a concave function in calculus.

Solution Method:

  1. Observe the relationship between the approximate function (straight lines) and the actual function (curve) in the figure.
  2. Compare the areas physically.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze the Figure:
    The diagram shows the actual function as a solid curve and the approximated function as a dotted line connecting points on the curve.
  2. Visual Inspection:
    Because the curve bulges outward (Concave Down), the straight lines connecting any two points on the curve sit strictly underneath the curve.
  3. Area Comparison:
    Since the trapezoids are contained entirely within the area under the curve (except at the vertices), the sum of the trapezoid areas must be less than the total area under the curve.\[\text{Area}_{\text{Trapezoidal}} < \text{Area}_{\text{Actual}} \]
  4. Mathematical Verification (Optional):
    The error term for the Trapezoidal rule is:\[E = -\dfrac{(b-a)^3}{12N^2} f''(\xi) \]For the curve shown, the slope decreases as \(x\) increases, so \(f''(x)\) is negative.
    \(E \propto -(\text{negative value}) \rightarrow \text{Positive Error}\)
    \(\text{Error} = \text{True Value} - \text{Approximate Value} > 0\)
    \(\therefore \text{True Value} > \text{Approximate Value}\)

Final Answer:

The numerical value of the area obtained using the trapezoidal rule will be less than the actual area.
Final Answer: (A) | Correct option: (A)

questions.question: Consider a doubly reinforced RCC beam with the option of using either Fe250 plain bars or Fe500 deformed bars in the compression zone. The modulus of elasticity of steel is \( 2 \times 10^5 \) N/mm². As per IS456:2000, in which type(s) of the bars, the stress in the compression steel ( \( f_{sc} \) ) can reach the design strength ( \( 0.87f_y \) ) at the limit state of collapse?
options: Both Fe250 plain bars and Fe500 deformed bars
Neither Fe250 plain bars nor Fe500 deformed bars

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: Both Fe250 plain bars and Fe500 deformed bars
structuredOptions.html: Both Fe250 plain bars and Fe500 deformed bars

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: Neither Fe250 plain bars nor Fe500 deformed bars
structuredOptions.html: Neither Fe250 plain bars nor Fe500 deformed bars

questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Structures | Limit State Method

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis (Material behavior in limit state design)
  • Given Data:
    • Doubly reinforced RCC beam
    • Steel Options: Fe250 (Plain) or Fe500 (Deformed)
    • Modulus of Elasticity: \(E_s = 2 \times 10^5 \text{ N/mm}^2\)
    • Code: IS 456:2000
  • Aim: Identify which steel grade can reach its full design strength \((0.87f_y)\) in the compression zone at the limit state of collapse.

Core Concepts:

  1. Strain Compatibility (IS 456:2000 Cl. 38.1):
    • Maximum Compressive Strain in Concrete: \(\epsilon_{cu} = 0.0035\)
    • Strain in compression steel \((\epsilon_{sc})\) is governed by the strain diagram: \(\epsilon_{sc} \leq \epsilon_{cu}\)
  2. Yield Strain of Steel:
    To reach the design stress of \(0.87f_y\), the steel strain must exceed the yield strain.
    • Fe250 (Mild Steel): Has a distinct yield point.\[\epsilon_y = \dfrac{0.87 f_y}{E_s} \]
    • Fe500 (HYSD/Cold Worked): No distinct yield point. Design stress \((0.87f_y)\) is reached at:\[\epsilon_{\text{target}} = \dfrac{0.87 f_y}{E_s} + 0.002 \]

Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the minimum strain required to reach design strength \((0.87f_y)\) for both steel grades.
  2. Compare these required strains with the maximum possible strain available from the concrete failure condition \((\epsilon_{cu} = 0.0035)\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze Fe250 (Plain Bars):
    \(f_y = 250 \text{ N/mm}^2\)
    Strain required to reach yield \((0.87f_y)\):\[\epsilon_{250} = \dfrac{0.87 \times 250}{2 \times 10^5} = \dfrac{217.5}{200000} \approx \mathbf{0.00109} \]
    Check availability: Since the concrete failure strain is 0.0035, and \(0.00109 \ll 0.0035\), compression steel situated close to the compression face will undergo strain greater than 0.00109.
    \(\therefore\) Fe250 yields and reaches design strength.
  2. Analyze Fe500 (Deformed Bars):
    \(f_y = 500 \text{ N/mm}^2\)
    Strain required to reach design stress \((0.87f_y)\) per IS 456 (Fig. 23):\[\epsilon_{500} = \dfrac{0.87 \times 500}{2 \times 10^5} + 0.002 \]\[\epsilon_{500} = \dfrac{435}{200000} + 0.002 = 0.002175 + 0.002 = \mathbf{0.004175} \]
    Check availability: The maximum possible strain (concrete crushing) is 0.0035.\[\epsilon_{\text{available}} \;(0.0035) < \epsilon_{\text{required}} \;(0.004175) \]Even if the steel were at the extreme fiber, the strain physically cannot reach 0.004175 before the concrete crushes.
    \(\therefore\) Fe500 never reaches full design strength \((0.87f_y)\) in compression.
  3. Conclusion:
    Only Fe250 plain bars can reach the design strength of \(0.87f_y\) in the compression zone.

Final Answer:

(A) Fe250 plain bars only
Final Answer: (A) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question: Consider the horizontal axis passing through the centroid of the steel beam cross-section shown in the figure. What is the shape factor (rounded off to one decimal place) for the cross-section?
questions.explanation:
Steel Structures | Plastic Analysis

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application (Calculation of Shape Factor)
  • Given Data:
    • Cross-section: Cruciform (Plus/+ shape)
    • Shape composed of 5 equal squares of size \(b \times b\)
    • Horizontal width \(= 3b\), Vertical height \(= 3b\)
  • Aim: Calculate the Shape Factor \((S)\).

Core Concepts:

  1. Shape Factor \((S)\): Ratio of Plastic Section Modulus to Elastic Section Modulus.\[S = \dfrac{Z_p}{Z_e} \]
  2. Elastic Section Modulus: \(Z_e = \dfrac{I_{xx}}{y_{\max}}\)
  3. Plastic Section Modulus: First moment of area about the Equal Area Axis (Plastic Neutral Axis).\[Z_p = \dfrac{A}{2}(\bar{y}_1 + \bar{y}_2) \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Geometry Definition:
    The cross-section consists of 5 squares each of area \(b^2\). Total height \(= 3b\). Due to symmetry, the Neutral Axis (NA) and Plastic Neutral Axis (PNA) both coincide at mid-height.
  2. Calculation of Moment of Inertia \((I_{xx})\):
    The section is split into three parts:
    • Part 1 – Middle horizontal strip (width \(= 3b\), height \(= b\)):​\[I_1 = \dfrac{3b \cdot b^3}{12} = \dfrac{3}{12}b^4 = 0.25\, b^4 \]
    • Part 2 – Top square (area \(= b^2\), centroid distance from NA \(= b\)):\[I_2 = \dfrac{b \cdot b^3}{12} + b^2 \cdot b^2 = \dfrac{1}{12}b^4 + b^4 = \dfrac{13}{12}b^4 \]
    • Part 3 – Bottom square (same as top square):\[I_3 = \dfrac{13}{12}b^4 \]
    \[I_{xx} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 = \dfrac{3}{12}b^4 + \dfrac{26}{12}b^4 = \dfrac{29}{12}b^4 \approx 2.417\, b^4 \]
  3. Calculation of Elastic Section Modulus \((Z_e)\):
    Distance to extreme fiber: \(y_{\max} = 1.5b\)\[Z_e = \dfrac{I_{xx}}{y_{\max}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{29}{12}b^4}{1.5b} = \dfrac{29}{18}\, b^3 \approx 1.611\, b^3 \]
  4. Calculation of Plastic Section Modulus \((Z_p)\):
    PNA is at the center (by symmetry). Moment of area of upper half:
    PartAreaCentroid distance from NAMoment
    Top Square\(b^2\)\(b\)\(b^3\)
    Top half of middle row\(1.5b^2\)\(0.25b\)\(0.375b^3\)
    Total——\(1.375\, b^3\)

    By symmetry, \(Q_{\text{lower}} = 1.375\, b^3\)\[Z_p = Q_{\text{upper}} + Q_{\text{lower}} = 2 \times 1.375\, b^3 = 2.75\, b^3 \]
  5. Calculation of Shape Factor:\[S = \dfrac{Z_p}{Z_e} = \dfrac{2.75\, b^3}{\dfrac{29}{18}\, b^3} = \dfrac{2.75 \times 18}{29} = \dfrac{49.5}{29} \approx 1.7068 \]\[\boxed{S \approx 1.7} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.7 | Correct option: (B)

questions.question: Consider the pin-jointed truss shown in the figure (not to scale). All members have the same axial rigidity, \( AE \). Members QR, RS, and ST have the same length \( L \). Angles QBT, RCT, SDT are all 90°. Angles BQT, CRT, DST are all 30°. The joint T carries a vertical load \( P \). The vertical deflection of joint T is \( k\dfrac{PL}{AE} \). What is the value of \( k \)?
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Deflection of Trusses

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Pin-jointed truss, all members have axial rigidity \(AE\)
    • Members QR, RS, ST each have length \(L\)
    • \(\angle QBT = \angle RCT = \angle SDT = 90^\circ\) (QB, RC, SD are vertical)
    • \(\angle BQT = \angle CRT = \angle DST = 30^\circ\)
    • Vertical downward load \(P\) at joint T
    • Vertical deflection at T: \(\Delta_T = k\,\dfrac{PL}{AE}\)
  • Aim: Find the value of multiplier \(k\).

Core Concepts:

  1. Truss Geometry: The specified angles define the inclination of the top chord members. The geometry means joints Q, R, S, T lie on a single straight inclined line.
  2. Zero-Force Members: Identifying members carrying no load to simplify analysis.
  3. Unit Load Method (Castigliano's Theorem):\[\Delta = \sum \dfrac{F_i\, u_i\, L_i}{AE} \]where \(F_i\) = force due to external load \(P\), \(u_i\) = force due to unit virtual load at T, \(L_i\) = member length.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Decoding the Truss Geometry:
    From \(\triangle SDT\) with \(\angle SDT = 90^\circ\), \(\angle DST = 30^\circ\), length \(ST = L\):\[SD = L\cos(30^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}L, \quad DT = L\sin(30^\circ) = \dfrac{L}{2} \]The entire top chord Q–R–S–T is a straight line at \(30^\circ\) with the vertical. Bottom chord panels:\[BC = CD = DT = \dfrac{L}{2} \]
  2. Force Analysis under Load \(P\) — Joint T:
    Top chord ST makes \(60^\circ\) with horizontal:\[\sum F_y = 0 \Rightarrow F_{ST}\sin(60^\circ) = P \Rightarrow F_{ST} = \dfrac{2P}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ (Tension)} \]\[\sum F_x = 0 \Rightarrow F_{DT} = -\dfrac{P}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ (Compression)} \]
    Since the top chord is a straight line and the load is only at T, all internal diagonals and verticals (SC, RB, SD, RC) carry zero force. The forces are uniform throughout each chord:
    • Top chord (QR, RS, ST): \(F = \dfrac{2P}{\sqrt{3}}\) (Tension)
    • Bottom chord (BC, CD, DT): \(F = -\dfrac{P}{\sqrt{3}}\) (Compression)
  3. Deflection via Unit Load Method:
    Apply unit vertical load at T; virtual forces mirror the \(F_i / P\) distribution:\[u_{\text{top}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \quad u_{\text{bottom}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \]
    Top chord contribution (3 members, each length \(L\)):\[\Delta_{\text{top}} = 3 \times \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2P}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)L}{AE} = 3 \times \dfrac{4PL}{3AE} = \dfrac{4PL}{AE} \]
    Bottom chord contribution (3 members, each length \(L/2\)):\[\Delta_{\text{bottom}} = 3 \times \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{P}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)}{AE} = 3 \times \dfrac{PL}{6AE} = \dfrac{0.5PL}{AE} \]
    Total Deflection:\[\Delta_T = \dfrac{4PL}{AE} + \dfrac{0.5PL}{AE} = \dfrac{4.5PL}{AE} \]
    Therefore, \(k = 4.5\).

Final Answer:

\(k = 4.5\) | Correct Option: (B)

questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Compaction

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Statements regarding soil compaction tests.
  • Aim: Identify the INCORRECT statement among the four options.

Core Concepts:

  • Compaction Curve: A plot of dry unit weight \((\gamma_d)\) versus moisture content \((w)\). The peak gives Maximum Dry Unit Weight and Optimum Moisture Content (OMC).
  • Effect of Compaction Effort: Increasing compactive effort (e.g., Standard → Modified Proctor) shifts the compaction curve upward and to the left — higher maximum \(\gamma_d\), lower OMC.
  • Zero-Air-Voids (ZAV) Curve: Represents the theoretical maximum \(\gamma_d\) at 100% saturation (no air voids).\[\gamma_{ZAV} = \dfrac{G\,\gamma_w}{1 + wG} \]

Evaluation of Each Statement:

  • (A) "Peak point gives maximum dry unit weight and OMC" — TRUE. This is the fundamental definition of the peak of the compaction curve.

  • (C) "With increase in compaction effort, OMC decreases" — TRUE. Higher energy forces particles closer together, requiring less water for maximum density.
  • (D) "Compaction curve crosses the zero-air-voids curve" — FALSE. Reaching the ZAV line requires 100% saturation. Mechanical compaction always leaves some entrapped air (saturation typically 85–95%). It is physically impossible for the compaction curve to touch or cross the ZAV line.

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
Consider that a force \( P \) is acting on the surface of a half-space (Boussinesq's problem). The expression for the vertical stress (\( \sigma_z \)) at any point \( (r, z) \), within the half-space is given as,
\[\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi} \dfrac{z^3}{(r^2 + z^2)^{\dfrac{5}{2}}} \]
where, \( r \) is the radial distance, and \( z \) is the depth with downward direction taken as positive. At any given \( r \), there is a variation of \( \sigma_z \) along \( z \), and at a specific \( z \), the value of \( \sigma_z \) will be maximum. What is the locus of the maximum \( \sigma_z \)?
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Stress Distribution in Soil

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Boussinesq's vertical stress expression:\[\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi} \cdot \dfrac{z^3}{(r^2 + z^2)^{5/2}} \]
    • \(r\) = radial distance (constant)
    • \(z\) = depth (variable)
  • Aim: Find the locus (relationship between \(r\) and \(z\)) where \(\sigma_z\) is maximized for a given constant \(r\).

Core Concepts:

Calculus — Maximization: To find the maximum of a differentiable function with respect to \(z\), set the first derivative \(\dfrac{\partial \sigma_z}{\partial z} = 0\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the differentiation:
    Let \(K = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi}\) (constant). Maximize:\[f(z) = z^3 \cdot (r^2 + z^2)^{-5/2} \]
  2. Differentiate with respect to \(z\) (product rule):\[\dfrac{df}{dz} = 3z^2(r^2+z^2)^{-5/2} + z^3 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{5}{2}\right)(r^2+z^2)^{-7/2} \cdot 2z = 0 \]
  3. Simplify:\[3z^2(r^2+z^2)^{-5/2} - 5z^4(r^2+z^2)^{-7/2} = 0 \]Divide both sides by \(z^2(r^2+z^2)^{-7/2}\) (assuming \(z \neq 0\)):\[3(r^2+z^2) - 5z^2 = 0 \]\[3r^2 + 3z^2 - 5z^2 = 0 \]\[3r^2 = 2z^2 \]\[\boxed{z^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}r^2} \]

Final Answer:

\(z^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}r^2\) | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A square footing of size 2.5 m × 2.5 m is placed 1.0 m below the ground surface on a cohesionless homogeneous soil stratum. Considering that the groundwater table is located at the base of the footing, the unit weights of soil above and below the groundwater table are 18 kN/m³ and 20 kN/m³, respectively, and the bearing capacity factor \( N_q \) is 58, the net ultimate bearing capacity of the soil is estimated as 1706 kPa (unit weight of water = 10 kN/m³).
Earlier, a plate load test was carried out with a circular plate of 30 cm diameter in the same foundation pit during a dry season, when the water table was located beyond the plate influence zone. Using Terzaghi's bearing capacity formulation, what is the ultimate bearing capacity (in kPa) of the plate?
questions.explanation:
Foundation Engineering | Bearing Capacity

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Square footing: \(B_1 = 2.5\text{ m}\), \(D_{f1} = 1.0\text{ m}\)
    • Water table at base of footing: \(\gamma_1 = 18\text{ kN/m}^3\) (above WT), \(\gamma_{sat} = 20\text{ kN/m}^3\), \(\gamma_w = 10\text{ kN/m}^3 \Rightarrow \gamma' = 10\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • \(N_q = 58\), cohesionless soil \((c = 0)\)
    • Net ultimate bearing capacity: \(q_{nu} = 1706\text{ kPa}\)
    • Plate load test: Circular plate, \(B_p = 0.3\text{ m}\), placed at pit base (surcharge \(= 0\))
    • WT beyond influence zone for plate test \(\Rightarrow\) use bulk \(\gamma = 18\text{ kN/m}^3\)
  • Aim: Find the ultimate bearing capacity \(q_u\) of the plate.

Core Concepts:

  • Terzaghi's formula — Square Footing \((c=0)\):
    Net ultimate capacity:\[q_{nu} = \gamma_1 D_f (N_q - 1) + 0.4\,\gamma'\, B\, N_\gamma \]
  • Terzaghi's formula — Circular Plate \((c=0,\; \bar{q}=0)\):\[q_u = 0.3\,\gamma_2\, B_p\, N_\gamma \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Extract \(N_\gamma\) from the footing data:\[1706 = (18 \times 1.0 \times (58-1)) + (0.4 \times 10 \times 2.5 \times N_\gamma) \]\[1706 = 18 \times 57 + 10\, N_\gamma \]\[1706 = 1026 + 10\, N_\gamma \]\[N_\gamma = \dfrac{680}{10} = 68 \]
  2. Calculate \(q_u\) for the plate load test:
    Circular plate at pit base: \(c=0\), \(\bar{q}=0\), \(\gamma_2 = 18\text{ kN/m}^3\), \(B_p = 0.3\text{ m}\):\[q_u = 0.3 \times 18 \times 0.3 \times 68 \]\[q_u = 1.62 \times 68 = 110.16\text{ kPa} \]
ParameterValue
\(N_q\)58
\(N_\gamma\) (back-calculated)68
\(B_p\)0.3 m
\(\gamma_2\)18 kN/m³
\(q_u\) (plate)110.16 kPa

Final Answer:

110.16 kPa | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A very wide rectangular channel carries a discharge (Q) of 70 m³/s per meter width. Its bed slope changes from 0.0001 to 0.0009 at a point P, as shown in the figure (not to scale). The Manning's roughness coefficient of the channel is 0.01. What water surface profile(s) exist(s) near the point P?
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Open Channel Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Discharge per unit width: \(q = 70\text{ m}^3/\text{s/m}\)
    • Initial bed slope: \(S_{01} = 0.0001\)
    • Final bed slope: \(S_{02} = 0.0009\)
    • Manning's roughness: \(n = 0.01\)
    • Channel: Very wide rectangular
  • Aim: Identify the water surface profiles upstream and downstream near slope transition point P.

Core Concepts:

  • Critical Depth: \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\)
  • Normal Depth (wide rectangular channel, \(R \approx y\)):\[q = \dfrac{1}{n}\, y_n^{5/3}\, S_0^{1/2} \]
  • Slope Classification: Mild (M): \(y_n > y_c\)  |  Steep (S): \(y_n < y_c\)
  • Profile Zones: Zone 2 on Mild slope → M2 (drawdown); Zone 2 on Steep slope → S2 (drawdown)
  • Control Section: At a Mild→Steep transition, flow passes through critical depth at point P.

Common Pitfall: Assuming a hydraulic jump occurs. A hydraulic jump only occurs at Steep→Mild transitions, not Mild→Steep.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Critical Depth \((y_c)\):\[y_c = \left(\dfrac{70^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{4900}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (499.49)^{1/3} \approx 7.93\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate Normal Depth for Slope 1 \((y_{n1})\):\[70 = \dfrac{1}{0.01} \times y_{n1}^{5/3} \times \sqrt{0.0001} = 100 \times y_{n1}^{5/3} \times 0.01 \]\[y_{n1}^{5/3} = 70 \Rightarrow y_{n1} = 70^{0.6} \approx 12.78\text{ m} \]Since \(y_{n1}\,(12.78\text{ m}) > y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\) → Slope 1 is Mild (M).
  3. Calculate Normal Depth for Slope 2 \((y_{n2})\):\[70 = 100 \times y_{n2}^{5/3} \times \sqrt{0.0009} = 100 \times y_{n2}^{5/3} \times 0.03 \]\[y_{n2}^{5/3} = \dfrac{70}{3} = 23.33 \Rightarrow y_{n2} = (23.33)^{0.6} \approx 6.64\text{ m} \]Since \(y_{n2}\,(6.64\text{ m}) < y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\) → Slope 2 is Steep (S).
  4. Identify Profiles:
    Point P is the control section where depth \(= y_c = 7.93\text{ m}\).
    • Upstream of P: Depth transitions from \(y_{n1}\,(12.78\text{ m})\) down to \(y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\). Depth lies between \(y_{n1}\) and \(y_c\) → Zone 2 on Mild slope → M2 profile (drawdown curve).
    • Downstream of P: Depth transitions from \(y_c\,(7.93\text{ m})\) down to \(y_{n2}\,(6.64\text{ m})\). Depth lies between \(y_c\) and \(y_{n2}\) → Zone 2 on Steep slope → S2 profile (drawdown curve).

Final Answer:

M2 and S2 | Correct Option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A jet of water having a velocity of 20 m/s strikes a series of plates fixed radially on a wheel revolving in the same direction as the jet at 15 m/s. What is the percentage efficiency of the plates? (round off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Impact of Jets & Hydraulic Machines

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Velocity of water jet: \(V = 20\text{ m/s}\)
    • Velocity of moving radial plates (wheel): \(u = 15\text{ m/s}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the percentage efficiency of the plates.

Core Concepts:

  • Series of Plates: For a wheel with a series of continuous plates, the entire jet mass strikes the plates per second: \(\dot{m} = \rho A V\).
  • Force on plates: \(F_x = \rho A V (V - u)\)
  • Power Output: \(P_{out} = F_x \times u = \rho A V (V-u)\, u\)
  • Power Input (KE of jet): \(P_{in} = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho A V^3\)
  • Efficiency:\[\eta = \dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} = \dfrac{2u(V-u)}{V^2} \]

Common Pitfall: Using the single moving plate formula \(\eta = \dfrac{2u(V-u)^2}{V^3}\) → gives incorrect \(6.25\%\). The keyword here is "series of plates fixed radially on a wheel".

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Apply the efficiency formula:\[\eta = \dfrac{2 \times u \times (V - u)}{V^2} \]
  2. Substitute values:\[\eta = \dfrac{2 \times 15 \times (20 - 15)}{20^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 15 \times 5}{400} = \dfrac{150}{400} = 0.375 \]
  3. Convert to percentage:\[\eta = 0.375 \times 100 = 37.5\% \]

Final Answer:

37.5% | Correct Option: (A)

    Column 2: I – Ponding, II – Freundlich Isotherm, III – Concentration Polarization, IV – Charge Neutralization
  • Aim: Correctly match each process in Column 1 with its associated mechanism in Column 2.

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
A plot of speed-density relationship (linear) of two roads (Road A and Road B) is shown in the figure.
If the capacity of Road A is \( C_A \) and the capacity of Road B is \( C_B \), what is \( \dfrac{C_A}{C_B} \)?
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Linear speed \((u)\) vs. density \((k)\) plots for two roads A and B.
    • Road A: Free flow speed \(= u_A\), Jam density \(= k_A\)
    • Road B: Free flow speed \(= u_B\), Jam density \(= k_B\)
  • Aim: Find the ratio of capacities \(\dfrac{C_A}{C_B}\).

Core Concepts:

Greenshields Model: Linear speed-density relationship:\[u = u_f\left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right) \]

Flow: \(q = u \cdot k = u_f\left(k - \dfrac{k^2}{k_j}\right)\)

Capacity (Maximum Flow): Obtained by setting \(\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0\):\[k_m = \dfrac{k_j}{2}, \quad u_m = \dfrac{u_f}{2} \]\[C = q_{\max} = u_m \cdot k_m = \dfrac{u_f \cdot k_j}{4} \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Capacity of Road A:\[C_A = \dfrac{u_A \cdot k_A}{4} \]
  2. Capacity of Road B:\[C_B = \dfrac{u_B \cdot k_B}{4} \]
  3. Ratio:\[\dfrac{C_A}{C_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{u_A \cdot k_A}{4}}{\dfrac{u_B \cdot k_B}{4}} = \dfrac{u_A\, k_A}{u_B\, k_B} \]
    The factor of \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) cancels out, giving the ratio directly in terms of the graph intercepts.

Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{C_A}{C_B} = \dfrac{k_A\, u_A}{k_B\, u_B}\) | Correct Option: (C)

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra – Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Analysis
  • Given Data:\[ [A] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \]
  • Aim: Identify the true statements regarding eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \([A]\), \([A]^T\), and \([A]^{-1}\).

Core Concepts:

  • Transpose Eigenvalues: \(\lambda([A]) = \lambda([A]^T)\), since \(\det(A - \lambda I) = \det(A^T - \lambda I)\).
  • Inverse Eigenvalues: If \([A]\) is invertible, \(\lambda([A]^{-1}) = 1/\lambda([A])\).
  • Inverse Eigenvectors: Eigenvectors of \([A]\) and \([A]^{-1}\) are identical.
    Proof: \([A]x = \lambda x \Rightarrow [A]^{-1}x = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}x\). The vector \(x\) is unchanged.
  • Transpose Eigenvectors: Eigenvectors of \([A]\) and \([A]^T\) are generally not the same unless \([A]\) is symmetric.

Common Pitfall: Assuming that because eigenvalues of \(A\) and \(A^T\) are the same, their eigenvectors must also be the same.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Verify Invertibility:\[|A| = 1(4-1) - 2(6-3) + 3(3-6) = 3 - 6 - 9 = -12 \neq 0 \]Matrix is non-singular; \([A]^{-1}\) exists.
  2. Statement (A): "Eigenvalues of \([A]^T\) are same as eigenvalues of \([A]\)"
    By \(\det(A - \lambda I) = \det(A^T - \lambda I)\), eigenvalues are identical. → TRUE
  3. Statement (B): "Eigenvalues of \([A]^{-1}\) are reciprocals of eigenvalues of \([A]\)"
    Standard property: \(\lambda(A^{-1}) = 1/\lambda(A)\). → TRUE
  4. Statement (C): "Eigenvectors of \([A]^T\) are same as eigenvectors of \([A]\)"
    Check symmetry: \([A]^T = \begin{bmatrix}1&3&3\\2&2&1\\3&1&2\end{bmatrix} \neq [A]\).
    Since \([A]\) is not symmetric, left and right eigenvectors are distinct. → FALSE
  5. Statement (D): "Eigenvectors of \([A]^{-1}\) are same as eigenvectors of \([A]\)"
    \([A]x = \lambda x \Rightarrow [A]^{-1}x = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}x\). Vector \(x\) is unchanged. → TRUE

Final Answer:

Statements (A), (B), and (D) are correct | Correct Options: A, B, D

questions.question: For the function \( f(x) = e^x |\sin x|; x \in \mathbb{R} \), which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The function is continuous at all \( x \)
The function is differentiable at all \( x \)

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: The function is continuous at all \( x \)
structuredOptions.html: The function is continuous at all \( x \)

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: The function is differentiable at all \( x \)
structuredOptions.html: The function is differentiable at all \( x \)

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus – Continuity and Differentiability

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data: \(f(x) = e^x |\sin x|\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\)
  • Aim: Determine which properties hold: continuity, differentiability, periodicity, boundedness.

Core Concepts:

  • Continuity: Product of two continuous functions is continuous.
  • Differentiability: \(|g(x)|\) is non-differentiable where \(g(x) = 0\) and \(g'(x) eq 0\).
  • Periodicity: \(f(x+T) = f(x)\) for all \(x\).
  • Boundedness: \(\exists\, M, N\) such that \(M \le f(x) \le N\) for all \(x\).

Note: In GATE MSQs, it is possible for only ONE option to be correct.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Continuity (Option A):
    \(e^x\) is continuous everywhere; \(|\sin x|\) is continuous everywhere.
    Their product \(f(x)\) is continuous for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). → TRUE
  2. Differentiability (Option B):
    Test at \(x = 0\) (where \(\sin x = 0\)):
    \( ext{RHD} = \displaystyle\lim_{h o 0^+} \dfrac{e^h \sin h}{h} = e^0 \cdot 1 = 1\)
    \( ext{LHD} = \displaystyle\lim_{h o 0^-} \dfrac{e^h(-\sin h)}{h} = e^0 \cdot (-1) = -1\)
    RHD \( eq\) LHD at \(x = n\pi\) → not differentiable everywhere. → FALSE
  3. Periodicity (Option C):
    \(f(x+\pi) = e^{x+\pi}|\sin(x+\pi)| = e^{x+\pi}|\sin x| = e^\pi \cdot f(x) eq f(x)\)
    The exponential factor \(e^x\) is strictly increasing; the function grows exponentially and never repeats. → FALSE
  4. Boundedness (Option D):
    At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\): \(f(x) = e^{\pi/2 + 2n\pi} \cdot 1 o \infty\) as \(n o \infty\).
    Function has no upper bound. → FALSE

Final Answer:

Statement (A) only | Correct Option: A

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Consider the beam shown in the figure (not to scale), on a hinge support at end A and a roller support at end B. The beam has a constant flexural rigidity, and is subjected to the external moments of magnitude \( M \) at one-third spans, as shown in the figure. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Bending Moment and Shear Force – Determinate Structures

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Simply supported beam, hinge at A, roller at B, total span \(= 3L\)
    • Constant flexural rigidity \(EI\)
    • Clockwise moment \(M\) at distance \(L\) from A; Anti-clockwise moment \(M\) at distance \(2L\) from A
  • Aim: Evaluate statements on reactions, shear force, bending moment, and deflection.

Core Concepts:

  • Static equilibrium: \(\sum F_y = 0\), \(\sum M = 0\)
  • Shear force: algebraic sum of vertical forces to one side of a section
  • Bending moment: algebraic sum of moments to one side of a section
  • Differential equation of deflection: \(EI\,\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = M(x)\); curvature exists wherever \(M(x) eq 0\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Support Reactions (Statement A):
    Take moments about A:\[R_B \cdot 3L + M - M = 0 \Rightarrow R_B = 0 \]\[R_A + R_B = 0 \Rightarrow R_A = 0 \]Both reactions are zero. → TRUE
  2. Shear Force (Statement B):
    With \(R_A = 0\) and no applied vertical loads, the sum of vertical forces on either side of any section is zero for \(0 \le x \le 3L\).
    \(V(x) = 0\) everywhere. → TRUE
  3. Bending Moment (Statement C):
    Using the left-hand side:
    • \(0 \le x < L\): \(M(x) = R_A \cdot x = 0\)
    • \(L < x < 2L\): \(M(x) = 0 + M = M eq 0\)
    • \(2L < x \le 3L\): \(M(x) = M - M = 0\)
    Bending moment is non-zero in the central region. → FALSE
  4. Deflection (Statement D):
    From \(x = L\) to \(x = 2L\): \(EI\,\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = M eq 0\).
    Non-zero curvature → beam undergoes pure bending and deflects in the central span. → FALSE

Final Answer:

Statements (A) and (B) are correct | Correct Options: A, B

options: D<sub>max</sub> is always equal to the height of the layer of unstable air

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution – Meteorology and Dispersion

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall & Comprehension
  • Given Data: Concept of Maximum Mixing Depth \((D_{\max})\) in atmospheric physics.
  • Aim: Identify correct statements regarding \(D_{\max}\), ventilation coefficient, and pollution potential.

Core Concepts:

  • Maximum Mixing Depth \((D_{\max})\): The maximum vertical height in the troposphere where vigorous convective mixing of air and pollutants occurs. Found by plotting the morning Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR) and drawing the Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) from the daily maximum surface temperature — their intersection gives \(D_{\max}\).
  • Ventilation Coefficient: \(= D_{\max} \times \bar{u}\) (mean wind speed within mixing depth). Measures the atmosphere's dispersive capacity.
  • Air Pollution Potential: Inversely proportional to the volume available for pollutant dispersion. Smaller \(D_{\max}\) → smaller dilution volume → higher pollution concentration.

Evaluation of Each Statement:

  • (A) "\(D_{\max}\) is always equal to the height of the unstable air layer" → FALSE. The instantaneous unstable layer height varies throughout the day. \(D_{\max}\) is the maximum height, typically reached in the mid-afternoon at peak surface temperature — not always equal to the current unstable layer height.
  • (B) "Ventilation coefficient depends on \(D_{\max}\)" → TRUE. Ventilation Coefficient \(= D_{\max} \times \bar{u}\), so it directly depends on \(D_{\max}\).
  • (C) "A smaller \(D_{\max}\) will have a smaller air pollution potential" → FALSE. Smaller \(D_{\max}\) traps pollutants in a smaller volume near the ground, increasing concentration and pollution potential.
  • (D) "Vertical dispersion of pollutants occurs up to \(D_{\max}\)" → TRUE. The mixing depth acts as an atmospheric lid (usually an inversion layer). Convective mixing and vertical dispersion occur freely up to this height but are suppressed beyond it.

Final Answer:

Statements (B) and (D) are correct | Correct Options: B, D

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
The differential equation,
\[\dfrac{du}{dt} + 2tu^2 = 1, \]
is solved by employing a backward difference scheme within the finite difference framework. The value of \( u \) at the \( (n-1)^{th} \) time-step, for some \( n \), is 1.75. The corresponding time \( (t) \) is 3.14 s. Each time step is 0.01 s long. Then, the value of \( (u_n - u_{n-1}) \) is ________________ (round off to three decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Differential Equation: \(\dfrac{du}{dt} + 2tu^2 = 1\)
    • Method: Backward difference scheme (Implicit Euler)
    • \(u_{n-1} = 1.75\) at \(t_{n-1} = 3.14\text{ s}\)
    • Time step: \(\Delta t = 0.01\text{ s}\)
  • Aim: Calculate \((u_n - u_{n-1})\).

Core Concepts:

Backward Difference (Implicit Euler) Approximation:\[\left.\dfrac{du}{dt}\right|_n \approx \dfrac{u_n - u_{n-1}}{\Delta t} \]The RHS function is evaluated at the current step \((t_n, u_n)\):\[\dfrac{u_n - u_{n-1}}{\Delta t} = f(t_n,\, u_n) \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine time steps:\[t_n = 3.14 + 0.01 = 3.15\text{ s} \]
  2. Discretize the ODE:\[\dfrac{u_n - u_{n-1}}{\Delta t} + 2t_n u_n^2 = 1 \]
  3. Substitute values:\[\dfrac{u_n - 1.75}{0.01} + 2(3.15)u_n^2 = 1 \]
  4. Rearrange into standard quadratic form:\[100(u_n - 1.75) + 6.3\,u_n^2 = 1 \]\[6.3\,u_n^2 + 100\,u_n - 176 = 0 \]
  5. Solve using the quadratic formula:\[u_n = \dfrac{-100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4(6.3)(-176)}}{2(6.3)} = \dfrac{-100 \pm \sqrt{10000 + 4435.2}}{12.6} \]\[u_n = \dfrac{-100 \pm \sqrt{14435.2}}{12.6} = \dfrac{-100 \pm 120.147}{12.6} \]
    • Root 1: \(\dfrac{20.147}{12.6} \approx 1.5989\) ✓
    • Root 2: \(\dfrac{-220.147}{12.6} \approx -17.47\) (physically unrealistic)
    So \(u_n = 1.5989\).
  6. Calculate the difference:\[u_n - u_{n-1} = 1.5989 - 1.75 = -0.1511 \approx -0.151 \]

Final Answer:

\(-0.151\) | Accepted key range: \(-0.152\) to \(-0.149\)

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: The infinitesimal element shown in the figure (not to scale) represents the state of stress at a point in a body. What is the magnitude of the maximum principal stress (in N/mm², in integer) at the point? ________________
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Principal Stresses

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Horizontal face (y-face): \(\sigma_y = 6\text{ N/mm}^2\) (Tensile), \(\tau_{xy} = 3\text{ N/mm}^2\)
    • Inclined plane at \(45^\circ\) to horizontal: \(\sigma_n = -4\text{ N/mm}^2\) (Compressive), shear stress magnitude \(= 5\text{ N/mm}^2\)
  • Aim: Magnitude of maximum principal stress \((\sigma_1)\).

Core Concepts:

Stress Transformation (Normal Stress on inclined plane):\[\sigma_n = \dfrac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} + \dfrac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\cos(2\theta) + \tau_{xy}\sin(2\theta) \]

Principal Stresses:\[\sigma_{1,2} = \dfrac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2} \]

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Define orientation:
    The inclined face normal is at \(\theta = -45^\circ\) from the x-axis, so \(2\theta = -90^\circ\).
    \(\cos(-90^\circ) = 0\), \(\sin(-90^\circ) = -1\).
  2. Find unknown \(\sigma_x\):\[-4 = \dfrac{\sigma_x + 6}{2} + \dfrac{\sigma_x - 6}{2}(0) + 3(-1) \]\[-4 = \dfrac{\sigma_x + 6}{2} - 3 \]\[-1 = \dfrac{\sigma_x + 6}{2} \Rightarrow \sigma_x = -8\text{ N/mm}^2 \]
  3. Calculate Principal Stresses:
    With \(\sigma_x = -8\), \(\sigma_y = 6\), \(\tau_{xy} = 3\):\[\sigma_{1,2} = \dfrac{-8+6}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{-8-6}{2}\right)^2 + 3^2} \]\[= -1 \pm \sqrt{(-7)^2 + 9} = -1 \pm \sqrt{49 + 9} = -1 \pm \sqrt{58} \]\[\sigma_1 = -1 + 7.616 = 6.616\text{ N/mm}^2 \approx 7 \]

Final Answer:

\(\sigma_1 \approx 7\text{ N/mm}^2\) | Accepted key range: 7 to 7

    By symmetry: \(R_{U_0} = R_{U_6} = 50\text{ kN}\) (\(\uparrow\))

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q56

questions.question:
A soil having the average properties, bulk unit weight = 19 kN/m³; angle of internal friction = 25° and cohesion = 15 kPa, is being formed on a rock slope existing at an inclination of 35° with the horizontal. The critical height (in m) of the soil formation up to which it would be stable without any failure is ________________ (round off to one decimal place).
[Assume the soil is being formed parallel to the rock bedding plane and there is no ground water effect.]
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Slope Stability – Infinite Slope / Planar Failure

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Bulk unit weight: \(\gamma = 19\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Angle of internal friction: \(\phi = 25^\circ\)
    • Cohesion: \(c = 15\text{ kPa}\)
    • Slope inclination: \(\beta = 35^\circ\)
    • Condition: Critical height at \(F_s = 1.0\)
  • Aim: Calculate the critical vertical height \(H\) (in m).

Core Concepts:

  • Stresses on the failure plane at depth \(H\):
    • Normal Stress: \(\sigma_n = \gamma H \cos^2\beta\)
    • Driving Shear Stress: \(\tau = \gamma H \cos\beta\sin\beta\)
  • Shear Strength (Mohr-Coulomb): \(\tau_f = c + \sigma_n\tan\phi\)
  • Stability condition at critical height: Driving stress \(=\) Resisting strength \((\tau = \tau_f)\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Equilibrium equation:\[\gamma H\cos\beta\sin\beta = c + (\gamma H\cos^2\beta)\tan\phi \]
  2. Trigonometric values:
    \(\cos 35^\circ \approx 0.8192\), \(\sin 35^\circ \approx 0.5736\), \(\tan 25^\circ \approx 0.4663\)
  3. Simplify driving term (LHS):\[\tau = 19H \times 0.8192 \times 0.5736 \approx 8.928H \]
  4. Simplify resisting term (RHS):\[\sigma_n\tan\phi = 19H \times (0.8192)^2 \times 0.4663 \approx 5.946H \]\[\tau_f = 15 + 5.946H \]
  5. Solve for \(H\):\[8.928H = 15 + 5.946H \]\[(8.928 - 5.946)H = 15 \]\[2.982H = 15 \Rightarrow H = \dfrac{15}{2.982} \approx 5.03\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

\(H \approx 5.0\text{ m}\) | Accepted range: 4.8 to 5.2

questions.question: A smooth vertical retaining wall supporting layered soils is shown in figure. According to Rankine’s earth pressure theory, the lateral active earth pressure acting at the base of the wall is ________________ kPa (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Earth Pressure – Rankine's Active Pressure (Layered Soil)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Surcharge: \(q = 20\text{ kPa}\)
    • Layer 1 (top 3 m): \(\gamma_1 = 18\text{ kN/m}^3\), \(\phi_1 = 32^\circ\), \(c_1 = 0\)
    • Layer 2 (bottom 4 m): \(\gamma_2 = 19\text{ kN/m}^3\), \(\phi_2 = 25^\circ\), \(c_2 = 20\text{ kPa}\)
  • Aim: Lateral active earth pressure at the base of the wall (depth \(z = 7\text{ m}\)).

Core Concepts:

Rankine's Active Pressure: \(p_a = K_a\,\sigma_v - 2c\sqrt{K_a}\)

Active Pressure Coefficient: \(K_a = \tan^2(45^\circ - \phi/2)\)

At the base, use Layer 2 properties \((\phi_2, c_2)\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate \(K_{a2}\) for Layer 2:\[K_{a2} = \tan^2(45^\circ - 12.5^\circ) = \tan^2(32.5^\circ) \approx (0.6371)^2 \approx 0.4059 \]
  2. Vertical stress at base \((z = 7\text{ m})\):\[\sigma_v = q + \gamma_1 h_1 + \gamma_2 h_2 = 20 + (18 \times 3) + (19 \times 4) \]\[= 20 + 54 + 76 = 150\text{ kPa} \]
  3. Active earth pressure at base:\[p_a = K_{a2}\,\sigma_v - 2c_2\sqrt{K_{a2}} \]\[= (0.4059 \times 150) - (2 \times 20 \times 0.6371) \]\[= 60.885 - 25.484 = 35.40\text{ kPa} \]

questions.question: A vertical trench is excavated in a clayey soil deposit having a surcharge load of 30 kPa. A fluid of unit weight 12 kN/m³ is poured in the trench to prevent collapse as the excavation proceeds. Assume that the fluid is not seeping through the soil deposit. If the undrained cohesion of the clay deposit is 20 kPa and saturated unit weight is 18 kN/m³, what is the maximum depth of unsupported excavation (in m, rounded off to two decimal places)? ________________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Excavation – Stability of Slurry Trench

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Surcharge: \(q = 30\text{ kPa}\)
    • Fluid unit weight in trench: \(\gamma_f = 12\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Clay: \(c_u = 20\text{ kPa}\), \(\gamma_{sat} = 18\text{ kN/m}^3\), \(\phi_u = 0\)
  • Aim: Maximum depth \(H\) of unsupported excavation.

Core Concepts:

  • Active Earth Pressure (soil side) for \(\phi = 0\), \(K_a = 1\):\[\sigma_a = \gamma_{sat}z + q - 2c_u \]Total active thrust:\[P_a = \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma_{sat}H^2 + (q - 2c_u)H \]
  • Fluid resistance (trench side):\[P_f = \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma_f H^2 \]
  • Limit equilibrium: \(P_a = P_f\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  2. Rearrange and divide by \(H\) \((H \neq 0)\):\[\dfrac{1}{2}(\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_f)H + (q - 2c_u) = 0 \]
  3. Substitute values:\[\dfrac{1}{2}(18 - 12)H + (30 - 40) = 0 \]\[3H - 10 = 0 \]

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 1 | CE Q59
